pl-l4d38c2-d1e115.summary: Distinguishes vows: common, like the baptismal promise to renounce the devil and his pomps; and singular, as when one freely promises to keep virginity, continence, or the like.
claims: Vows are common or singular.

pl-l4d38c2-d1e118.summary: Distinguishes singular vows: private, made in secret, and solemn, made before the Church; violating a private vow is mortal sin, violating a solemn one is sin and scandal.
claims: Breaking a private vow is mortal sin; a solemn one adds scandal.

pl-l4d38c2-d1e121.summary: Holds that those who privately vow continence should not marry, since they sin mortally by doing so; yet if they do, they are not separated, since what was done secretly cannot be proved; those who vow solemnly can by no means marry, and for them not only marrying but even wishing to is damnable.
claims: Private vows make marriage sinful but valid.
Solemn vows invalidate marriage.

pl-l4d38c2-d1e125.summary: Quotes Augustine: in the conjugal bond, if chastity is kept, damnation is not feared; but in widowed continence and virginal excellence a greater gift is sought; once sought, chosen, and vowed, not only marrying but even wishing to marry is damnable.
claims: After a vow of continence, even the wish to marry is damnable.

pl-l4d38c2-d1e137.summary: Cites Paul to Timothy: avoid younger widows, who when wanton wish to marry in Christ, having damnation because they made void their first faith, even by willing, not marrying; the will fallen from its purpose is damned whether marriage follows or not; and if they are damned for wishing to marry, marriages they actually contract must be voided and they recalled to their purpose.
claims: Vowed widows who wish to marry break their first faith.
Marriages contracted against a vow must be voided.

pl-l4d38c2-d1e155.summary: Quotes Gregory: widows who abandon their purpose of widowhood are damned by Paul unless they convert; we judge them excommunicated and barred from the church until they obey their bishops and return, willingly or not, to the good they began.
claims: Vowed widows who abandon their purpose are excommunicated.

pl-l4d38c2-d1e164.summary: Quotes Innocent on unveiled virgins who stray: those not yet veiled who always professed to remain virgins must do penance for a time if they marry, since their promise was held by the Lord; if contracts of good faith among men cannot be dissolved, how much less a promise made with God without punishment.
claims: Even unveiled virgins who vowed and marry must do penance.

pl-l4d38c2-d1e171.summary: Adds: if unveiled virgins are so punished, much more widows of mature age and counsel who took the religious habit and then apostatized and returned to their vomit must be excluded from the church and the faithful until satisfaction, and given to prison.
claims: Professed widows who apostatize are punished more severely.

pl-l4d38c2-d1e177.summary: Concludes that virgins or widows bound by a vow of continence, veiled or not, can by no means marry, and the same holds of all who vowed continence: what was lawful before becomes unlawful after the vow.
claims: A vow of continence makes marriage unlawful.

pl-l4d38c2-d1e181.summary: Cites Innocent's decree: widows and girls who spiritually married Christ and later publicly married are not to be admitted to penance until those they joined have departed this world; for if a woman who marries another while her husband lives is an adulteress without license for penance until one dies, much more she who first joined the immortal Bridegroom and then turned to human marriage.

pl-l4d38c2-d1e187.summary: Interprets Innocent as not excluding from penance those who wish to repent worthily, but those who will not leave the incestuous union; one who neglects to return to her profession cannot be reconciled; the man 'dies' to her when she wholly withdraws from his unlawful embraces.
claims: Penance is denied only to those who persist in the illicit union.

pl-l4d38c2-d1e193.summary: States that the following comparison declares and confirms this sense.

pl-l4d38c2-d1e196.summary: Explains that when husband and wife are lawfully joined, neither can pass to another union while the other lives without adultery; Clement says nothing is graver than adultery, which holds second place in punishment after those who stray from God. Adulterers sin most gravely, fornicators gravely, the incestuous more gravely, and those who sin against nature most of all.
claims: Adultery is graver than fornication.
Incest is graver than adultery.
Sin against nature is gravest.

pl-l4d38c2-d1e202.summary: Quotes Augustine: adultery surpasses fornication but is surpassed by incest; but the worst of all is what is against nature, as unnatural use of a woman, execrable in a harlot but more so in a wife.
claims: Unnatural acts are worst, worse in marriage than outside it.

pl-l4d38c2.summary: Distinguishes common vows, like baptismal renunciation of the devil, from singular ones, like vowing virginity; singular vows are private or solemn: breaking a private vow is mortal sin, breaking a solemn one sin and scandal. Those who vow continence privately sin mortally by marrying, but are not separated, since a secret vow cannot be proved; those who vow solemnly cannot marry at all, and even to will it is damnable, as Augustine and Paul on young widows show. Gregory and Innocent impose excommunication and penance on vowed widows and virgins who marry. Innocent's denial of penance to them until their partners 'die' means until they leave the illicit union. Adultery is graver than fornication, incest graver than adultery, and sin against nature gravest, even with one's wife.
claims: Vows are common or singular, private or solemn.
Breaking a private vow is mortal sin; breaking a solemn one adds scandal.
A private vow makes marriage sinful but not invalid; a solemn vow invalidates it.
Vowed persons who marry must be separated and do penance.
Sins against nature are graver than incest, adultery, and fornication.
